You can't really optimize the trial and error feedback loop time.

I think it will look more like Claude just helping every expert along the way do their job better. Analyzing and synthesizing data to make better experimental suggestions and design new equipment (or totally new experiments based on unconceived-of apparatuses?). Labs already are artificial environments that make organisms have odd phenotypes, and odd interactions which bias the data away from what you’d find in the natural world.

You add in robotic manipulation, and you add a new confound.

Drones in the wild are an obvious counterbalance to this, though even in that scenario, the drone can be a confound unless well hidden.

In the end though, this kind of systemic breakdown of biology, while much needed raw material to improve our theories, won’t solve the whole of biology. Human hands and human minds will be needed for a good long while.

My reading of the hypothesis is this, interested in your thoughts:

> unless you can create a magical classifier

A generator could concentrate on pockets while remaining unable to judge most drugs. And LLM RLVR a) works well, and b) is black box optimisation and so is suited since it doesn't need system identification (which you can't do for complex biological systems). So the hypothesis is that, yes making a classifier is very very hard, but you could through some (lots?) initial interactive data, end up with our generator outputting with high probability drugs-that-end-up-passing-trials-with-probability-p. Whether these drugs thus generated are drugs we care about (i.e, whether `p` is good enough) and whether the whole pocket it generates in is large enough, and how jagged this behaviour is (i.e distribution of `p` across taxonomies of drugs), are the few questions we want answered.

Well first off: molecular screening (which is basically what you're describing) is inadequate for drug discovery. There are too many other factors that matter: water positions, molecular flexibility, short and long-range electrostatics, entropy loss, coordinating ions, and more. You need not only the "pocket", but an accurate model of the system's conformational change over time, to have any hope of understanding binding energetics. It's a bigger problem for small molecule drug discovery than biologics, but it still matters.

That said, we have extremely well-refined force fields that attempt to model the underlying physics, and still fail to do this well. There's absolutely no reason to believe that a generic LLM will bring anything to the table that improves the situation. Even with the hand-wavy assertion that we (somehow) get "lots and lots of data", and somehow train a purpose-built model to do the same, it's kind of like saying that we could turn a minivan into a formula one car with enough effort. Different tools for different jobs.

I actually do believe that informatics approaches will be helpful given lots of system-specific data, but when I say that, I mean "a bespoke neural energetic model that is trained specifically for some molecular system down to customized force-field parameters", not "Claude".

So sure, maybe Anthropic will invest lots of time and money and energy into making these kinds of molecular simulation models, which they can then use for high-throughput screening experiments. But even if they do all of that, there's still no guarantee that they'll bring anything to the party that hasn't been done before...because this is the lowest-value step of drug discovery, and a model like that won't tell you if your drug is going to be toxic, or have off-target effects, or have metabolic problems, or...a million other things, which are what kill drug programs in phase 1 and beyond.

I'll bite: why not?

The good: smartest people I have ever worked with, though also some of the dumbest (think of a saddle curve rather than a bell curve :-). Really interesting, fun, and really super-hard technical problems.

Discouraging-but-part-of-life issues: nobody is in a rush because everything is a marathon. It typically takes decades to get anything into the market; though regulators over the past few decades have been changing things to speed things up (basically doing science to make the process more adaptive and dynamic) it's still hard. You're continually looking for needles in haystacks: wispy signals that may be noise, extracted from huge datasets. As a startup, expensive slow, e.g. an overnight session on an HPLC can be a $10,000 experiment (or more because you're probably running a lot of those instruments in parallel at once) after having a bunch of people working all day to prep the samples.

The terrible: the industry is riven top to bottom with fear. Fear that the science will not work out. Fear that someone else is smarter than you (as a result: pervasive arrogance and hostility). Fear in the FDA that some company trying to game the system* will get something past you, or that the inspector general will launch an investigation, or some congressperson will launch a missile at you for no legitimate reason.

Also, you're launching artillery shells that can't be altered in flight. You write a study and then you have to run it with the protocol you wrote and got approved. You can't alter your marketing message unless it refers to scientific results explicitly demonstrated in a trial. And since the trials typically take years, there's a lot of sitting around.

* Back when I was in the biz we absolutely did not try to game the system and it made it a lot easier to work with the Agency (FDA). But the rules kept being made tighter and tighter to lock our bad action by companies. The system I built was called exacycle. It ran as a borg job in every cluster we had access to, with priority 0 or 1, with N tasks (where N=# of machines in the cluster). Borg ran the "worker" task as long as there were resources free on the machine (often, several workers ran on the same machine, and no workers ran on other machines). There was a global schedulers that picked mini-tasks off a global queue and fed them to the cluster-level scheduler (batches based on instant resource availability, and subject to some data locality optimization) which then fed them to the machine workers.

At peak, we had 1-3 million xeon cores running our tasks (protein folding, protein design, drug docking), 24/7. This was before GPUs were really a thing. Each mini-task was basically a rosetta or gromacs or autodock binary running on local inputs and writing local outputs for ~1 hour using ~1GB RAM and no network. Input and output was via colossus, or distributed through a global torrent network (literally all 1-3 million cores formed a single data transfer group, with data passed between clusters at low probability).

I built most of the code of the system (which depended on Google infra) including the scheduler and the machine worker, and also ran the system as on-call "SRE" for 3 years. During that time, we nearly almost didn't take down the Google global network, and had small latency impacts on many services. Managing to run the system for so long without antagonizing ads or search or youtube was a major challenge.

I would say the complexity of the system I built (considering everything down to the OS) was roughly the level of a few human cells in a plate, in terms of interacting components and the complexity of their interactions.

We actually need that AND labeled trial outcomes, which is a challenge in and of itself because pharma companies will often hide negative trial results (which are advantageous for training the model layer) in order to exacerbate the perception of drugs that make it to market (search for "missing data phenomenon pharma"). The clinical trials are an extremely costly (and necessary) market inefficiency that leads to a bunch of bad behavior that is unfortunately self-reinforcing. I spoke on the phone with a biotech entrepreneur who told me to think of the Gavin Belson (from Silicon Valley the TV show) quote where he says "I don't know about you, but I don't want to live in a world where someone other than me makes the world a better place better than me", and to just remember that's how many people think in pharma and biotech + pharma.

Augmenting how pharma companies work is a great first step. Augmenting how candidate drugs are engineered is a good first step. But that does not change the fact that we simply do not have deterministic governing laws (as we do in physics) to understand the complete pharmacokinetics/dynamics of a drug across a large patient population. You just have to run the test. It is true that AI will help, but only as much as we have a reasonable way to predict that candidate drugs will lead to positive trial outcomes and a large market.

Note that I am not a doomer here. I think AI will have a profoundly disruptive and positive impact on the pharma industry. I'm just not sure starting with drug design alone leads to hope unless there are things happening in the background between pharma + the labs (very possible) that could lead to better trial outcomes.
